newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy mourns death of another cinema great.
newsitem.headline: Italy mourns death of another cinema great.

text.p: Italy mourned the passing of yet another of its cinema greats on Saturday with the death of director Giuseppe De Sanits, one of the fathers of Italian postwar film.
De Santis, perhaps best known for his sensual masterpiece "Riso Amaro" (Bitter Rice, 1949), died in Rome's Sant'Eugenio hospital late on Friday after a heart attack, hospital sources said. He was 80.
"He had great dramatic breadth coupled with an uncommon technical capacity," said veteran actor Vittorio Gassman, who starred in "Bitter Rice" alongside sex symbol Silvana Mangano.
"He had a natural imagination which could transfigure everyday life and happenings thanks also to his expertise in handling the camera," Gassman said.

De Santis, who helped write Luchino Visconti's 1942 classic "Ossessione" (1942), was a champion of neorealism, which sought to highlight the miseries of Italian life following World War Two and the Fascist regime of dictator Benito Mussolini.

"In his films and in those he worked on, he told the story of the drama of the war, of Italy being rebuilt, of the Italy that was still rural in the 1950s," Culture Minister and vice premier Walter Veltroni said in a telegram to De Santis's wife.
"The images of his films remain among the most beautiful of our cinema," Veltroni said.

Director of 11 films in 25 years, De Santis's other main works include "Caccia Tragica" (Tragic Hunt, 1947) and "Non c'e pace fra gli ulivi" (Under the Olive Tree, 1950). Both pleaded for improved social conditions in postwar Italy.

His death came just one week after another great Italian director, Marco Ferreri, died from a heart attack aged 69 in Paris, and about five months after the passing of legendary Italian actor Marcello Mastroianni at the age of 72.
"De Santis was a great poet of workingmen and farmers," Gilles Jacob, director of the Cannes Film Festival, was quoted by Italian news agencies as saying in the French city.
"After Mastroianni and Ferreri, another great artist of Italian cinema has gone," he said.
While praised as a hero of neorealism, some also considered De Santis -- who had not directed a film since 1972 -- to have heralded its end.

Neorealism, whose greatest exponents were directors Roberto Rossellini and Vittorio De Sica, gradually fizzled out in the 1950s as Italian cinema succumbed to an increasing trend for escapist entertainment.

"Bitter Rice", a melodramatic and sensual story set in the rice fields of the northern Po Valley, launched the prolific career of Mangano and was regarded by some as a commercial exploitation of the socially committed style.

"The image of Mangano, with her stockings rolled up to her thighs, her dizzying shorts, and voluptuous bosom...is one of the most erotic symbols in cinema...of all times," Italian news agency ANSA said.

Director Carlo Lizzani, who collaborated with De Santis on his three best-known works, said he owed his own professional success to the elder filmmaker, who was given a lifetime achievement award at the Berlin Film Festival in 1995.

"Italian cinema owes him much, for his great films which marked the beginning and evolution of neorealism as well as for the coherence and integrity that characterised his professional life," Lizzani said.
